where: the page-level outage strip, and the same component in its wrapped form on sync-orphaned
finding: The strip now has a measure but it still has no right edge. In the three states where the actions fit beside the message — queued, failed, differs — the content runs to the strip's inner edge and the object reads as composed. In the two states where it does not, the same component leaves a dead column the full height of the strip: the message is capped at its 480px maximum, the actions are set immediately after it or wrapped underneath at the left padding, and nothing at all occupies the remainder. On sync-outage that remainder is 407px — a third of the loudest object on the page, and the one that governs the whole screen — sitting empty beside a six-line paragraph. It reads as a banner that was sized for a wider layout than the one it got, which is the opposite of the impression a screen-wide condition should give.
evidence: sync-outage: the strip spans x 256–1408 (1152px); its content spans 274–1001. Six text lines end at x 950 and the actions column ends at 1001; x 1001–1408 is empty over all 160px of strip height. sync-orphaned: strip 512–1152, content 528–997 — 155px dead over 290px of height. Compare sync-profile, sync-failed and sync-differs, where content reaches 1136 of an 1136 inner edge.
direction: Give the strip two ends at every width rather than one. When the actions can sit beside the message, push them to the strip's far edge so the gap between them reads as a gutter rather than a leftover; when they cannot, let the message give up its cap and take the full width so the paragraph shortens instead of the strip growing a void. Either way the rule to hold is that the strip's right edge is always occupied by something.

where: every glyph-led block — the notice and the held-field group in sync-blocked, the strip on sync-orphaned
finding: The leading state glyph creates a hanging indent for the prose, and then every non-prose sibling in the same block ignores it and aligns to the container's own padding instead. So each of these blocks has two left edges about 25px apart, and the element that hangs left is always the one the sentence is answering: the button sits outboard of the paragraph that justifies it, the field labels sit outboard of the sentence that explains them. Nothing here is a legible choice — the indent is an accident of putting an icon in a flex row — and it costs the blocks their sense of being one object, because the eye finds a stepped left margin where it expects a spine.
evidence: sync-blocked: the ◌ sits at x 486, the notice's heading, body and caption all start at 510, and 'Create her in Planning Center' starts at 483. The held group repeats it — its amber sentence starts at 495, the 'First name' label directly under it at 481. sync-orphaned: the paragraph starts at 552, the one-new-person caption and the 'Re-create her in Planning Center' pill both at 528.
direction: Pick one spine per block and hold everything to it. Either treat the glyph as a gutter, in which case the button and the fields indent to the prose edge too, or let the glyph sit only with the heading and return the body to the container edge on the second line. The first reads better here, because the glyph is then a marker on the block rather than a character in the sentence.

where: the grade and last-seen columns down the roster, right of the middle band
finding: The middle band was made into columns and the right of the row was not. Grade and last-seen are right-aligned facts, and their right edges take three and four different values down the list depending on how many standing flags the row happens to carry — a row with two chips pushes both columns 28px left of a row with one. On the screen whose entire argument is 'read down forty-five rows', two of the four fact columns wander, and they wander for a reason the reader cannot see, since the thing causing it is the width of chips further right. Against the newly-straight caption edge in the middle band it is conspicuous: the left half of the row is now a table and the right half is still a flex row.
evidence: sync-students fold, grade right edges: 1216 on Ava, Marcus, Benson, Sofia, Eli, Noah, Zoe, Amara, Bea, Caleb, Daniela; 1198 on Priya (two chips); 1188 on Kai, Jonah, Aiden (two chips). Last-seen right edges: 1121, 1120, 1102, 1093 on the same pattern. 'No grade' on Kai ends 28px left of '9th grade' on the row above it.
direction: Finish the row the way the band was finished: give grade and last-seen set right edges of their own and let the flag cluster absorb its own variation, rather than letting a two-chip row pay for itself out of the columns to its left. The cluster's reserved width should be a floor sized to its busiest row, not to its median.

where: the ‖ (waiting) and ! (failed) marks in the job family, at 11px
finding: Six separable silhouettes was the right target and the set nearly reaches it — ▪, →, ✓, ≠, ⊘ and ◌ are genuinely far apart — but two of them are the same shape, and they are the pair that most needs not to be. Stripped of hue, ‖ renders as a solid vertical bar with no gap between its two strokes (the gap is sub-pixel at this size, so the 'pause' metaphor it was chosen for is not on the glass at all) and ! renders as the same vertical bar with a 2px break near the baseline. So the state that resolves itself and the state that will not resolve without a human are separated by two pixels of counter, and what actually tells them apart is the colour and the word — which is what the glyph was introduced to spare the reader.
evidence: sync-students fold, glyphs converted to luminance and magnified 20×: the waiting mark on Marcus's row is a 4×11px filled bar; the failed mark on Benson's row is a 4×11px bar with one dark row near the bottom. Against them, the queued ▪ is a 7×6px square and reads as a different class immediately. The same ! carries all ten held rows on sync-outage.
direction: Take one of the two out of the vertical-bar class. The failed state is the one that has to survive a glance, so give it the silhouette that no other mark shares — a triangle, a filled disc, something with mass rather than a stroke — and leave the bar to waiting, where the reader has time. Test at 11px in greyscale, not at 6× in colour: if two marks are indistinguishable with the hue removed, the hue is doing the work.

where: the rank inside the mark family — '! Save failed · 1wk' against '✓ Saved · just now' and '▪ Queued · 14s'
finding: The rank landed for one of the two states that need a human and not for the other. '≠ Changed upstream · 2m' is now correctly the widest and heaviest mark in the table, and shortening the routine words pulled queued, waiting and sending down where they belong. But the failure did not come up to meet it: it was shortened along with them, and because danger sits far below present and warn on this ramp, the mark for the edit that has been refused for a week now carries less optical mass than the mark for a save that completed a second ago and than the mark for an edit that is fourteen seconds old. Inside the family that means 'yours to resolve', the two members differ by more than the members of that family differ from the ones that need nothing.
evidence: Chip widths on the fold: 'Changed upstream · 2m' 180px, 'Saved · just now' 134px, 'Save failed · 1wk' 133px, 'Sending · 40s' 115px, 'Queued · 14s' 111px, 'Waiting · 1m' 106px. Measured ink mass above the row background: differs 74k, saved 72k, sending 71k, waiting 71k, queued 70k, failed 58k — the failure is the lightest job mark in the column. Peak luminance 142 on danger against 184 on present and 200 on warn.
direction: The instruction was to let the two states that persist keep the width, and only one of them did. Give the danger pair a common floor so they read as one rank — the age is the part that earns the width on a week-old failure, so it can be said in full rather than abbreviated. And take the width back off the landed state instead: a mark nobody needs to read is the one that should be shortest in the family, and 'Saved' alone says everything 'Saved · just now' says.

where: 'Keep Ito' / 'Send Chen-Ito again' in the strip and 'Edit profile' below it, and the two-up they resolve
finding: Making the two choices matched secondaries was right and it has left the page with three identical objects: the two halves of the decision and the record's routine navigation are the same fill, height, radius and type, so the screen offers three peers where it means to offer one question and one aside. Separately, the choice and the comparison it resolves are laid out on perpendicular axes in different parts of the strip — the values sit side by side across the full width at the bottom, the buttons sit stacked at the top right — so the reader has to re-map left/right onto top/bottom, and the pair only holds together because the labels repeat the values. Having gone to the trouble of making the values the figure, the strip then answers them somewhere else.
evidence: sync-differs fold: 'Keep Ito', 'Send Chen-Ito again' and 'Edit profile' all sample #1e293b. The buttons occupy x 943–1136, y 179–256; the cells they choose between occupy x 528–828 and 836–1136, y 338–414. The 'ON THE RECORD NOW' cell is ringed danger and its button is 150px above and to the right of it.
direction: Bind each choice to the value it chooses — put the action inside or immediately beneath its own cell so the pair reads as one object with two halves and the axis of the choice matches the axis of the comparison. And when the strip deliberately declines to have a primary, the record's routine action needs to step down a further rank rather than sitting level with the decision, so the page keeps an order in this state as it does in the other four.

where: the bold runs inside the 'Marcus Webb is editing this record too' notice
finding: Bold is doing two unrelated jobs in one six-line paragraph, and the less important job is winning. The field names Marcus is changing — 'Last name', 'Grade' — are bold because they are the facts. Then a fifty-eight-character instruction about where to look is bold too, and because it runs across a line and a half it is by some way the heaviest block of ink in the notice: squint and the notice reads as a heading plus a bold slab in the middle, with the two field names dissolved into the body around it. The reader is being shouted at about the mechanism and told quietly about the content.
evidence: sync-editor fold, notice at y 90–248: 'Last name' and 'Grade' are 9 and 5 bold characters on line 1; 'each of those boxes says underneath what he is changing it to' is bold across the ends of line 3 and all of line 4. The same weight is used for both.
direction: One meaning per weight. Keep bold for the values and field names the reader has to take away, and set the instruction plain — or drop it to the caption rank, where the notice already puts secondary detail on the other scenes. The hints under the boxes now carry the values, so the sentence pointing at them can afford to be quiet.

where: "Planning Center's" in the standing note and the held-group label, against "Tally’s own" four lines above
finding: Two kinds of apostrophe are on the glass at once in the same modal, in the same class of sentence. The set is otherwise consistently typeset with curly quotes — the refusal message's quoted reason, 'Ava’s record', 'Amara Whitfield’s new record', 'Tally’s Planning Center connection' — so the three straight ones read as text that came from a different keyboard than everything around it. It is small, and it is the kind of small that undoes the impression of care the rest of the type is building.
evidence: sync-blocked: 'Notes and roster status are Tally’s own' (curly, 14px bold) at y 195, then "Name, grade, birthday and allergies are Planning Center's" (straight, 12px) at y 344 and "Planning Center's six fields, held until Amara's record exists" (straight ×2, 12px amber) at y 634. sync-editor carries the third at y 272.
direction: Normalise to the curly apostrophe the rest of the copy already uses.
